articles.title: Daily EU public tender alerts in Google Sheets with the free TED API
articles.excerpt: The EU publishes every above-threshold public tender on TED (Tenders Electronic Daily), and it offers a free search API that needs no API key. This post builds a small job that: asks TED for tenders m…
articles.body: The EU publishes every above-threshold public tender on TED (Tenders Electronic Daily) , and it offers a free search API that needs no API key. This post builds a small job that: asks TED for tenders matching your CPV codes and countries, keeps only notices that are new or changed since the last run, appends them to a Google Sheet every morning. 1. Can I reuse TED data? Yes. The Publications Office's legal notice ( https://ted.europa.eu/en/legal-notice ) says procurement notices "can be freely reused, for commercial or non-commercial purposes", and its editorial content is under CC BY 4.0. That means you credit the source and say what you changed. Don't use the TED logo.

articles.title: You Want to Ask to Work Four Days a Week
articles.excerpt: You have done the sums. With a little less money you could have Fridays back, for your children, your health, a parent who needs you, or simply a life with some air in it. What stops you is not the mo…
articles.body: You have done the sums. With a little less money you could have Fridays back, for your children, your health, a parent who needs you, or simply a life with some air in it. What stops you is not the money. It is the worry that asking will quietly mark you as someone who is no longer serious about their career. That worry is worth taking seriously, and it is also worth testing, because it is often bigger than the reality. Find out the rules first. Look in your handbook for a flexible working policy, and check whether anybody on your team or nearby already works reduced hours. In the UK, since April 2024, employees can make a formal flexible working request from their first day, up to two in any twelve months, and the employer has to respond within two months.

articles.title: Terraform said no changes and our Lambda kept running last month's code
articles.excerpt: In March one of our suppliers changed the date format on their delivery notes, and the Lambda that parses them started rejecting every one. We fixed the parser that afternoon. The pull request was rev…
articles.body: In March one of our suppliers changed the date format on their delivery notes, and the Lambda that parses them started rejecting every one. We fixed the parser that afternoon. The pull request was reviewed, CI built the package, terraform apply ran green, and the next morning the Lambda was still rejecting the notes. Its logs showed a stack trace from a line we had deleted. The function is an aws_lambda_function whose filename points at build/delivery-parser.zip. Until February the zip name carried the build number, so every build changed the filename attribute and Terraform updated the function code. A tidy up gave the zip a fixed name, and from then on apply reported No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration. It was right.

articles.title: Changing a Mobile Number in Our HR Portal Was Enough to Take Over an Account
articles.excerpt: Our HR system has a self service portal where employees view payslips, book holiday and update their personal details. When it went live it was given its own username and password rather than our sing…
articles.body: Our HR system has a self service portal where employees view payslips, book holiday and update their personal details. When it went live it was given its own username and password rather than our single sign on, because the supplier charged extra for the integration and the portal was thought to hold nothing an attacker would want. Two years later we connected it to our identity system, so that a new starter's details would flow across automatically. One of the fields that flowed across every night was the personal mobile number. Our self service password reset uses that number to send a code. It seemed sensible: HR held the most accurate number for each person, so the reset would always reach them.

articles.title: How to stop an AI agent from overspending: a 6-step checklist (2026)
articles.excerpt: Disclosure: I work on Pink Agentic AI Payments at PinkWallet, a spend-control layer for AI agents. The numbers below come from two open datasets (linked) and from the official documents cited; Pink is…
articles.body: Disclosure: I work on Pink Agentic AI Payments at PinkWallet, a spend-control layer for AI agents. The numbers below come from two open datasets (linked) and from the official documents cited; Pink is mentioned once, at the end, as one example. Short answer: you stop an AI agent from overspending by putting the limit outside the model : give the agent no raw card, give each agent its own budget, check every payment at the moment it executes, send exceptions to a person (and decline if nobody answers), cap how fast it can spend, and test all of it with fake money first. A sentence like "never spend more than $50" in the system prompt is not a limit: the model can misread it, forget it, or be talked out of it by a prompt injection.

articles.title: mcp-doctor: one open-source tool for the whole life of an MCP server
articles.excerpt: An agent is only as reliable as the tools it calls, and most MCP servers are never checked against anything. A tool with no description never gets picked. A parameter typed str = None rejects the very…
articles.body: An agent is only as reliable as the tools it calls, and most MCP servers are never checked against anything. A tool with no description never gets picked. A parameter typed str = None rejects the very default it advertises. A write tool says "Successfully wrote" and writes nothing. I built mcp-doctor to catch those, and it has grown into one open-source tool that covers an MCP server's whole life: before you ship, in every PR, and inside the running agent. 1. Before you ship pip install mcp-server-lint mcp-doctor path/to/your/server Lint. Reads Python, TypeScript and Go source without running it, and grades quality and security separately, so a well-documented server can't hide a security gap behind one blended number.

articles.title: Scientists find 'gemstones' in atmosphere of bizarre, scorching-hot 'marshmallow' exoplanet
articles.excerpt: Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers have unravelled some of the secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot exoplanet that has the consistency of marshmallow.
articles.body: Using data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have unraveled some of the atmospheric secrets of a bizarre, blisteringly hot world that has the consistency of marshmallow. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , under the watchful infrared eye of the JWST , is WASP-17b, located around 1,300 light-years away. The exoplanet has a mass around 0.8 times that of Jupiter, but it is around twice as wide as the solar system's largest planet, giving it a "super-puff" consistency comparable to the Earth-based treat. WASP-17 b is so close to its parent star that it completes an orbit in under four Earth days, with this proximity also making the temperature of this " hot Jupiter " skyrocket.

articles.body: If you love watching meteors, 2026 has given you plenty to enjoy. And there's more to look forward to: in December, the Geminids, the year's most prolific shower, will peak after a waxing crescent moon sets early in the evening, opening the door to excellent viewing. Right between those two headline showers, the dependable Orionids take their turn, reaching peak activity around Oct. 21-22. So, when and where can you catch the show? When and where to watch Make sure you wrap up warm for a night of Orionid hunting.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 16, 1975: NASA launches the 1st-ever GOES weather satellite to watch Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 16, 1975, NASA launched the first operational GOES weather satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 16, 1975, NASA launched the first operational GOES satellite! GOES-A was the first in a series of weather satellites that NASA jointly operated with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The name is short for Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite . GOES-A launched on a Delta rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida. GOES satellites all have a geostationary orbit, which means they always face the same part of Earth — in this case, the Indian Ocean. Once GOES-A became operational, it was renamed GOES-1. The GOES satellite fleet has grown over the years, and is a critical link in the chain of satellites tracking Earth's weather from space.
